The Sand roller (Percopsis transmontana) attains an ultimate fork length of 10.3 cm [Li = 10.3 cm], a size typical for a small-bodied freshwater percopsid inhabiting the Columbia River basin. Field surveys indicate that individuals reach this maximum dimension only after several years of somatic growth, with most adults measured in gill-net samples clustering between 8 and 10 cm. The species exhibits a relatively modest maximum body mass, with the heaviest individuals recorded at an ultimate wet weight of approximately 17 grams [Wwi = approximately 17 grams], a value consistent with the slender, fusiform body shape that facilitates foraging in moderate currents. At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low at 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], reflecting the small diameter of the demersal, adhesive eggs from which the yolk-sac larvae emerge. This initial mass, equivalent to roughly 0.00015 of the ultimate adult mass, is among the smallest size ratios observed in North American freshwater teleosts and implies a highly altricial developmental trajectory from the moment of chorion rupture onward.

During the early phases of development, the transition from endogenous to exogenous nutrition marks a critical period of high mortality for the prolarvae. At a sustained water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal regime commonly recorded in the species' natal streams during late spring, the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at approximately 292 days [tp = approximately 292 days]. This value was derived from von Bertalanffy growth models fitted to length-at-age data for individuals reared under controlled laboratory conditions that mimicked natural thermal regimes. The attainment of a fork length at puberty of 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm] serves as the morphological benchmark for this transition, signaling the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the beginning of vitellogenesis in females. This length threshold is reached only after the individual has completed the juvenile growth phase, during which the yolk-sac larva transforms into an actively feeding fingerling capable of capturing copepods and aquatic insect larvae.

Reproductive investment in the Sand roller is closely tied to body size, with field studies revealing that females measuring 9.1 cm in fork length exhibit a mean daily egg production rate of approximately 9.2 eggs per day  when maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This rate was calculated from direct counts of ovulated eggs stripped from gravid individuals captured during the spawning season and is substantially lower than the species' theoretical maximum. The maximum reproductive rate recorded for this species reaches 14.7 eggs per day [Ri = 14.7 eggs per day] under the same thermal conditions, a value observed only in the largest and most energetically robust females. These data suggest that the allocation of resources toward gamete production increases disproportionately with length, likely reflecting the greater body cavity volume and higher foraging intake rates achievable by larger individuals.

Longevity estimates derived from otolith-based age determination indicate that the maximum lifespan of Percopsis transmontana is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when individuals experience the typical thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] prevalent in their mid-elevation stream habitats. This age is considerably longer than that reported for many co-occurring cyprinids and reflects a relatively slow life-history pace characterized by delayed reproduction and iteroparous spawning over multiple seasons. The majority of mortality occurs during the first year of life, with high predation pressure from piscivorous salmonids and sculpins eliminating a large fraction of the young-of-year cohort before they reach the 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm] fork length threshold associated with puberty. Among those that survive to adulthood, senescence becomes apparent after the fourth year, when growth rates slow markedly and the incidence of fungal infections on the fins increases.

Comparative analyses with other members of the family Percopsidae reveal that the Sand roller's life-history strategy falls at the slower end of the continuum, with a reproductive output that is more modest than that of its congener, the trout-perch (Percopsis omiscomaycus). At a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at puberty of 292 days [tp = 292 days] is roughly 30 percent longer than that reported for trout-perch populations in the Great Lakes, suggesting that the Sand roller's montane environment imposes a constraint on developmental rate. The wet weight at birth of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams] is virtually identical between the two species, indicating a conserved egg size that reflects the constraints of yolk provisioning in demersal spawning. The combined evidence of an asymptotic adult mass of 17 grams [Wwi = 17 grams] and a maximum documented lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] places the Sand roller as a moderately long-lived, slow-growing species relative to its body size within the broader percopsid clade at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].
